THE UNITED NATIONS DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK IN
THE PHILIPPINES
 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1. The UNDAF in the Philippines initiates a United Nations reform process focusing on
enhanced inter-agency collaboration in order to optimize the contributions UN development
programmes can make to the government and people of the Philippines.
2. The main implementors of the UNDAF in the Philippines are the 10 United Nations agencies,
composed of the JCGP group, UNDP, UNFPA, and UNICEF, the Specialized Agencies,
FAO, ILO, UNESCO, UNHCR, UNIDO and WHO, and a special program, UNAIDS.
Forming the UN Country Team under the leadership of the Resident Coordinator, the agency
heads have examined the kinds of collaborative approaches they undertook previously,
especially in relation to UN global conferences, assessed the strengths and weaknesses of
these experiences, and have taken steps to accelerate a collaborative process that goes beyond
mere sharing of information. This process was greatly facilitated by the intense interest and
action taken by the government and NGOs in the subjects highlighted by the global
conferences, and the sophisticated levels of data collection and analysis already existing in
the Philippines
3. The Country Strategy Note has been a mainstay of the UNDAF process, as have the
numerous meetings held with government and non-governmental organizations to prepare for
the 10 global conferences and carry out post-conference implementation. Strategies, action
plans, indicators, and monitoring and evaluation schemes were formulated in such detail that
they were judged as equivalent to the Common Country Assessment. Drawing on the many
lessons learned through these consultations, as well as from ongoing programme and project
collaboration, the UNCT feels confident that UNDAF in the Philippines can move
systematically to more integrated ways of working. Although UNDAF evaluation will focus
on those activities in which several agencies are involved, these being the more experimental
ones that require careful review, the UNCT has affirmed that single-agency managed
programmes remain an integral and important part of the UN system. Further, all UN
programmes and projects, whether multiple or single in character, fall under UNDAF’s
purview.
4. While UNDAF as a process largely entails the involvement of UN System agencies, its
successful outcome will be seen in effective government and civil society programmes
addressing the country’s priority needs effectively, especially in the social areas. The
Philippines has exhibited significant economic progress over the past ten years, yet a high
proportion of its population falls below the poverty line. The Asian currency crisis has
generated serious apprehension about the country’s future in the midst of drought, poverty
and globalization. The newly elected President has pledged to focus his efforts on the rural
and urban poor, while striving to sustain economic growth through greater liberalization.5
Given the fairly modest levels of assistance afforded the country through the UN System,
agency heads position their efforts strategically for maximum impact. The UN capitalizes on
its particular niches, bringing its global experience to bear on the needs of sustainable human
development.
5. The UNDAF process centres around four Strategic Areas of Cooperation encompassing 12
Priority Areas for UN Collaboration and five Cross-Cutting Themes. These are the
following, together with their agency convenors:
Strategic Area of Cooperation No. 1. Economic Growth with Equity. Priority Areas for
Collaboration: Small and medium industries (UNIDO), Sustainable livelihood (UNDP)
Strategic Area of Cooperation No. 2. Human Development, Human Rights and Human
Resource Development. Priority Areas for Collaboration: Education (UNESCO), Food
security and nutrition (FAO), Child labour (ILO), Empowerment of women (UNICEF),
Reproductive health (UNFPA), Indigenous people’s empowerment (ILO), Peace building
(UNDP/Resident Coordinator), and HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS)
Strategic Area of Cooperation No 3. Environment and Sustainable Development. Priority
Area for Collaboration: Industry and environment (UNIDO)
Strategic Area of Cooperation No. 4. Governance and Development Management. Priority
Area for Collaboration: Governance (UNDP)
Cross-Cutting Concerns to be examined in each Strategic Area of Cooperation are: protection
and promotion of child rights, environment, gender, capacity building and social equity.
6. Twelve Inter-Agency Working Groups (IAWG), each led by an agency head, have been
formed to intensify multi-agency interaction around the 12 priority areas for collaboration and
cross-cutting themes. These activities are viewed as part of the learning process for UNDAF
development, and meant to be flexible and experimental. The UNCT will monitor IAWG
results through regular reporting from the convenors at inter-agency meetings, and act on
recommendations for changes needed in programmes, policies, evaluation schemes,
administrative and financial matters. Country programme mid-term and end-of-cycle reviews
offer other opportunities for monitoring progress on collaboration, as do the annual work
planning sessions of the Resident Coordinator and UNCT.
7. While each agency is responsible for carrying out its share of the UNDAF responsibilities,
the Resident Coordinator’s Office, located on UNDP premises, shepherds the process and
provides staffing and logistic support to the agencies engaged in jointly planned collaborative
activities under the UNDAF. The UN Country Team is a managing a minimum of
US$140 million to support the implementation of UNDAF.6
THE UNITED NATIONS DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE
FRAMEWORK IN THE PHILIPPINES
 I. THE UNDAF PREPARATION PROCESS
The Philippines: A Pilot Country
1. The United Nations family welcomed the designation of the Philippines as one of the first
11 UNDAF pilot countries to participate in the UN reform process. Already known for
its working Resident Co-ordinator System and productive inter-agency activities, the UN
Country Team (UNCT) saw the Secretary-General’s initiative as giving further impetus to
re-examining and strengthening programmes and projects within a new strategic
framework for expanded collaboration at country level.
2. Because the Government and NGO sectors took strong initiatives in regard to United
Nations global conferences, UN agency roles in the Philippines focused on influencing,
guiding and supporting its government and civil society partners in the preparations,
conference negotiations, and post-conference implementation and monitoring. These
complementary actions enabled the Philippines to generate exemplary national plans of
action for the various UN global conferences1
, and establish a solid base for follow-up
activities. The UN System continued to provide post-conference continuity and to support
a common agenda for action.
3. UN System assessments of specific problems and approaches focused on the six theme
groups organised in 1996 to integrate global conference commitments into agency
programmes in the Philippines. Multi-stakeholder groups devoted their attention to
sharing information on basic social services, the advancement and empowerment of
women, environment and sustainable development, employment and sustainable
livelihood, rural development and food security, and HIV/AIDS. These task forces made
recommendations for each area, situating them also in the broader framework of
sustainable human development. Shared accounts of field-level experiences furnished
illustrative cases that highlighted opportunities and constraints linked to collaboration.
The Common Country Assessment (CCA)
4. The UN Country Team has been engaged with government and civil society groups over
the last few years in an intensive assessment of problems and strategic issues that has
strongly influenced the directions of UN development assistance. (See Figure 1.) These
ongoing UN Country Team efforts were facilitated by well-developed government
planning systems and the availability of sophisticated data bases. Agreement was reached
on indicators that were most important to the UN System. (See Figure 2). UNDP,
 
1 For a listing of these UN System global conferences, see table on page 137
UNICEF and UNFPA have each gone through intensive data analysis as part of their
country programming processes.
5. Information for common country assessments evolved as agency heads and their staffs
participated in one another’s country programme preparations and periodic reviews,
jointly developed the UNDP Country Advisory Note together with the Country Strategy
Note (CSN), and worked to integrate global conference results into national programmes.
Together, the UN Country Team formulated and approved the 1997 goals of the Resident
Co-ordinator System in the Philippines, forged the beginnings of a common services
budgeting strategy, and created a UN program on post-conflict development and peacebuilding efforts in Mindanao. Thus, the main functions of the CCA had already been
accomplished when UNDAF’s CCA guidelines were received.
6. In reviewing the UNDAF guidelines to determine whether the requirements of a CCA had
already been met, the UNCT concluded that compliance had, in effect, been achieved
through these recent exercises. Instead of preparing a formal CCA, therefore, the Team
preferred to highlight as an equivalent contribution, the processes and substantive
outcomes that had emerged from its collective assessment of problems, global conference
recommendations, and Philippine Government and NGO priorities. This multi-sectoral
analysis further clarified the courses of action each agency would subsequently undertake
separately and collaboratively. The outcome was judged by the UNCT as having met the
CCA’s first criterion of “Scope.” The second criterion, “Participation,” had been
similarly addressed through the intensive work of the Inter-Agency Task Forces around
environment and sustainable development, basic social services, the empowerment of
women, HIV/AIDS, and sustainable livelihoods. The third criterion, “Common Ground,”
had also been covered through the Inter-Agency Task Forces, made up of UN,
Government and NGO focal points, and through the incorporation of their output into
regular country planning, programming and project development exercises.
7. Drawing on the equivalent CCA, the Country Team transformed the UNDAF exercise
itself into a forward-looking mechanism for reformulating country needs, strategies and
priority actions into a dynamic development assistance framework for inter-agency
collaboration in 1998-99. Twelve Inter-Agency Working Groups were organised, each
led by an agency head, around 12 priority areas. These were classified under five
strategic thrusts and integrated through five cross-cutting themes. (See paragraph 59)
Periodic evaluations of their results over the coming years will serve as the basis for the
UNCT’s CCA and framework for collaboration.
8. Eleven sets of indicators have been selected to guide this process, corresponding to the
areas in which the UN System is concentrating its assistance in the Philippines. Gender
and age criteria are incorporated into the key and sub-indicators to ensure the centrality of
women’s and children’s concerns in any review of data. The 11 indicator areas which
subsume specific monitoring criteria (see annexes) start with overall well-being seen in
human and gender development, gender empowerment and children’s rights measures,
population, mortality, health, education, income and employment, children in especially
difficult circumstances, access to clean water and sanitation, food security, environment
and ecosystems, and governance.8
Organising for UNDAF
9. UN Country Team consultations got underway immediately upon receipt of the SecretaryGeneral’s 14 July 1997 message and guidelines from various agency headquarters. They
first sought to understand UNDAF as a process and, as stated in Headquarters guidelines,
as a framework for action rather than a joint programme. The regular UN monthly
meetings, chaired by the Resident Co-ordinator, determined the steps needed to move the
collaborative process itself forward and to generate the Philippine UNDAF report.
10. With UNDAF concepts and procedures fairly well defined by the end of 1997, the ten
member UN country team held a two-day workshop in January 1998 to agree on a work
plan and timetable for the UNDAF report, identify priority areas and procedures for
collaboration based on the recommendations of the theme groups, and develop
mechanisms for mobilising the staff toward greater collaboration.
11. The period following the January workshop saw several follow-up actions. Agency heads
shared and discussed the UNDAF workshop report with their respective partners and staff
to keep them abreast of progress. Selected government agencies were also furnished
copies to ensure their understanding of the process. The two United Nations
Headquarters facilitators who visited Manila in January were impressed by the group
spirit, the strong will to collaborate, and the Resident Co-ordinator’s efforts to strengthen
teamwork. They made several suggestions on the workshop report and carried back to
New York the Country Team’s views on ways in which the UNDAF process could be
enhanced. As agreed at the January meeting, the Resident Co-ordinator convened four
additional one-day workshops from February to May to review the drafts of the UNDAF
report. These gatherings had the effect of further clarifying concepts about UNDAF
among the various agencies and getting agreement on work plans, timetables and
procedures for moving ahead.
12. As a result of these discussions, the Country Team reached a consensus on the major
development challenges facing the Philippines and ways in which the United Nations
agencies, funds and programmes could best address them, recognising their individual
and collective comparative advantages. These workshops had assessed past attempts at
collaboration in terms of strengths and weaknesses, advantages and disadvantages,
opportunities and constraints. The resulting four major strategic thrusts encompassing
twelve priority areas and five cross-cutting concerns will serve as the dynamic framework
for new working arrangements aimed at more effective UN inter-agency collaboration.
13. Even as the Country Team sought to broaden and deepen collaboration, they affirmed that
discrete single- or dual-agency programmes geared to particular sets of mandates would
continue to play important roles in UN assistance. While these efforts would not be
monitored in the same way as programmes and projects calling for active collaboration
among three or more agencies, greater effort would nonetheless be made to harmonise
these single or dual programmes within the overall UNDAF framework. At the same
time, the drive toward collaborative programming would move away from mere9
information sharing to a mode of actively working together for greater convergence
toward common goals reached through planning, implementing, monitoring and
evaluating together. The results would generate a more synergistic impact than is
possible for single or dual programmes. (See Figure 3.) In the end, whether single, dual
or multi-agency, it is the vision behind these programmes and the common framework
integrating them that give unity to UN System activities in the Philippines.
 II. DEVELOPMENT CHALLENGES FACING THE PHILIPPINES
National Development Goals
14. In the 21st century, the Philippine Government’s stated development vision is “to create a
modern and humane society, raise the quality of life for all Filipinos -- children, youth,
women and men alike -- and bequeath this society in an ecologically healthy state to
future generations. This society is politically mature, peaceful and united as a nation. The
families, as the basic units, lead lives of prosperity, dignity and freedom.” 2
The Philippine
National Development Plan for the 21st century aims to fashion a society where “per
capita income adjusted for inflation is sufficiently high, grows at a steady rate, and is not
easily eroded by population growth and unforeseen shocks, whether internal or external.
It envisions a society where poverty is absent. The distribution of income and wealth is
fair and acceptable, helping preserve social cohesion.”
15. The plan emphasises the importance of “an industrialisation strategy that involves the
modernisation of agriculture, industry and services. In raising the standards of living of
all citizens, the plan emphasises the centrality of raising the productivity of agriculture
and the incomes of families dependent on it. It recognises the need to invest in human
capital. It is conscious of the fact that modernisation poses risks to the environment and
natural resources. Thus, the plan also advocates fighting entropy by protecting these
precious resources as the country grows. The plan upholds decentralisation and
devolution with the enactment of the Local Government Code. It shuns heavy
government intervention in the economy and relies on market competition and the price
system through liberalisation, deregulation and privatisation and continued adherence to
democratic political institutions.”3
16. The Government has signed a number of international human rights treaties as a sign of
its commitment to people’s well-being. This means that the Government must report
annually on progress in each of these areas and can thus be held accountable for its
compliance with, for example, the 1951 Convention and 1967 Protocol relating to the
Status of Refugees; International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; the Convention
on the Elimination of All forms of Discrimination against Women; the Convention on the

Rights of the Child; the Convention on the Minimum Age for Employment (Child
Labour) and other ILO Conventions on basic human rights. In addition, the Philippine
Government agreed to undertake the human development agenda adopted in the World
Summit for Social Development (Copenhagen), the International Conference on
Population and Development (Cairo), the Fourth World Conference on Women (Beijing),
the Second International Conference on Shelter and Human Settlements (Istanbul), the
Earth Summit (Rio de Janeiro), and Earth Summit+5 (New York), the International
Conference on Nutrition (Rome) and the UN General Assembly Declaration of the
Decade for Human Rights (1995-2005).4
17. The reality against which this vision is articulated poses many challenges to the
Government’s ambitious goals, yet offers promise toward their achievement. The
positive elements emerge in the economic recovery, which began in 1992 accompanied
by a broad series of policy reforms. This in turn led to a steady rise in growth and
renewed optimism about the Philippines’ re-establishing its position as an economically
viable Asian country. Anticipating the status of Newly Industrialised Country (NIC) by
the year 2000, the Government launched development policies aimed at bringing
economic growth and an improved quality of life to all Filipinos.
18. The political environment for these policies has been reinforced by improvements in
peace and security. The signing of the peace agreement with the Moro National
Liberation Front ended decades of conflict in Mindanao. The peace process has also been
strengthened by progress in peace negotiations with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
and the National Democratic Front of the Communist Party of the Philippines. Another
form of peaceful accommodation with a strong human rights linkage appears in the
resolution of the Vietnamese refugee problem. Numbering some 300,000 over 20 years,
most have found new countries for settlement or were repatriated to Vietnam. Vietnamese
who could not or would not leave the country have been allowed to remain and are now
integrated into the local population, often with Filipino spouses.
18. The ensuing political stability, coupled with structural adjustment and stabilisation
reforms, ushered in a period of high-performing growth. Driven by stronger exports and
investment, gross national product (GNP) progressed from negative growth in 1985 to a
positive 0.8 per cent in 1992 and 6.8 per cent in 1996. A per capita GNP of US$1,085
was achieved three years ahead of schedule in 1995.5
 Available statistics indicate the
Government poverty eradication programmes, along with economic growth, have been
instrumental in reducing the incidence of poverty. From 49 percent in 1961, the
percentage of the population in poverty decreased to 39.9 per cent in 1991 and, further, to
35.5 per cent in 1994. The number of poor families was thus reduced by about 250,000
in the latter three years. At the same time, the inequitable distribution of wealth and the
large number of families remaining in a state of poverty loom as continuing concerns.

20. In the sphere of employment, government figures indicate that an estimated 1.5 million
jobs were created during 1995, and employment grew by 2.6 percent. However, these
figures must be tempered by considering that the actual number of jobs created in wage
employment in 1995 came to about 662,000, according to the statistics of the Department
of Labour and Employment. There is an average of 600,000 to 700,000 new entrants in
the labour force every year. Hence those who remain unemployed either participate in
unpaid family occupations, work overseas or join the informal sector.
21. Despite significant progress in the economy, when statistical accounts are disaggregated
to differentiate women’s situations from those of men, the gender gap emerges all too
visibly. Many more women than men are in low-paying, low-skilled activities.
Occupational segregation channels women into less remunerative and less productive
segments of the labour market. Wage remuneration as well as access to credit and land
resources remain unequal. An increasing shift away from large centralised workplaces
towards more decentralised work arrangements, such as subcontracting and using the
home as a work site, exacerbate the problem of low-paying jobs for women. This kind of
work also offers little by way of non-wage benefits, job security or protection against
work hazards. Moreover, the likelihood of the woman’s combining her economic work at
home with domestic chores and childcare is bound to increase work intensity and stress.
The trend for poor women to remain in the informal service sector leads to jobs that are
not monitored or regulated and therefore susceptible to work hazards. Women overseas
contract workers, who now form the majority in this category, face inadequate worker
protection, high stress and potential victimisation in often hostile foreign settings.
22. The human development index (HDI), for the Philippines, an aggregate measure of
welfare, improved from .621 in 1992 to .672 in 1994. The Gender Empowerment
Measure (GEM), which captures the extent to which women are able to participate
actively in the economic and political life of the country, also showed improvement
between 1995 and 1996. Reproductive health conditions are better, for example, with
modern contraceptive use moving from 24.9 per cent in 1993 to 30.9 per cent in 1997,
and maternal mortality declining substantially.6
 However, the Gender Development Index
(GDI) revealed consistently low values prevailing in all regions of the country.7
 Some
regions even reported a decline in their GDI between 1990 and 1994, a pattern largely
traceable to significant income differences between women and men. Gender disparity,
or the percentage reduction of the GDI from the Human Development Index, was greatest
in Western and Central Mindanao, but even the National Capital Region showed a GDI
that was only half its HDI.
23. In the 14 per cent of households headed by women, the feminization of poverty loom
large. Although women-headed households in the upper and middle-income groups show
higher incomes than comparable male-headed households, those in the bottom 40 per cent
record average household incomes of about P2000 less than the average P14,678 male-

24. The situation of children as a whole is also more promising. After decades of poor
performance, infant mortality declined from 56.7 per 1000 births in 1990 to 48.9 in 1993,
and under-five child mortality from 79.6 per thousand children in 1990 to 66.8 in 1995.9
Malnutrition rates are also lower, while literacy rates have risen, along with access to safe
water supply and sanitation. When data on children are disaggregated by gender,
however, disturbing trends emerge that show girls as often worse off than boys.
Nutritional levels place girls of 7-10 years as consistently more underweight and stunted
than boys. Anaemia among 13-19 year olds affects females more than males (35.9 vs.
26.3%), while goitre is found in 6.1 per cent of females 13-20 years compared to 0.1 per
cent among the equivalent males. In 1990 the maternal mortality rate for young mothers
under 15 years was 592.3 per 100,000 live births, compared to an already high 180 for
adult mothers. Studies on family and household violence reveal that almost all child
abuse victims are young girls (96.5 %), a majority (58.3 %) of them between 11-17 years,
the average age being 11. The highest incidence of abuse involves rape and sexual
exploitation (69 % of cases), followed by other forms of physical abuse (20 % of cases).10
25. Although progress has been made in the recognition, protection and promotion of the
rights of children and women, disturbing trends are evident. Large differentials by
province characterise infant, child and maternal mortality, with the five high mortality
provinces showing rates that are twice those of the five lowest provinces. Some exhibit
malnutrition levels two or three times the national level. Rising literacy is offset by the
consistently low cohort survival rates for elementary schooling (68 per cent) and a similar
rate for secondary education. Girls remain longer in the school system, however, than
boys. Enormous differences appear between the National Capital Region encompassing
Metropolitan Manila, with elementary school survival rates over 80 per cent, and postconflict regions in Mindanao, whose rates range from 36 per cent to 59 per cent.
26. In the 5-17 age categories, working children constitute 3.7 million, or 16 per cent. This
means that one out of six Filipino children between the ages 5-17 is a working child.11

Some 215,561 working children are between 5-9 years old. Child domestic workers are
overwhelmingly girls, as are child sex workers. Street children, on the other hand, are
composed largely of boys. Among the different forms of child abuse reported, the most
common is sexual exploitation (69 per cent of cases) and physical abuse (20 percent of
cases).12 Six per cent, or 2.2 million working children, are threatened by hazardous work
environments marked by physical hardship and exposure to poisonous chemicals. They
suffer from work-related problems of exhaustion, stress, risk and danger. Twenty-four
per cent, or 869,199 of the overall population of children, contract an illness or at least
one work-related injury. Thirty per cent, or 600,000 do not attend school. Those boys
and girls who are in school, especially in rural areas, face high educational costs, distance
and difficulty in catching up with lessons.
27. While efforts are underway to address these inequities in line with the Philippines’ Social
Reform Agenda, major challenges threaten the country’s capacity to sustain its human
development trajectory. The recent Asian currency crisis has heightened the vulnerability
of the country’s banking and financial sectors to fluctuations in regional exchange rates. It
has shown the need to adapt to the changes brought about by global integration involving
trade in commodities, securities, and national currencies. This has affected investments,
exports and employment, and cut deeply into government budgets in a period of declining
ODA and decreasing revenues. Already, GNP growth rates decreased to 5.8 per cent by
late 1997, with further declines predicted. Government has been obliged to cut back 25
per cent of the budget across-the-board. The currency crisis also threatens environmental
and social programmes, raising the prospect that the government’s vision of sustainable
human development will remain an elusive dream.
28. Pressures to increase exports threaten measures taken to limit natural resource
degradation. Also affected is implementation of the Social Reform Agenda, which aims at
attacking social inequities through asset reform, a just sharing of the benefits of growth,
and the active participation of ordinary men and women in the political and economic
mainstream. Targeted at the poorest groups – landless agricultural workers, small-farm
cultivators, fisherfolk, indigenous cultural communities, urban informal sector workers
and the urban poor, the disabled, and women, youth and children in all these categories –
the SRA entails intensive consultations between government, NGOs and people’s
organisations (POs). NGOs and POs insist that what is needed now is to go beyond
rhetoric and planning to actual implementation. 13
29. Most likely to suffer as a result of the looming economic downturn are the Filipino poor.
Government reports indicate that over four million households were well below the
poverty line in 1994. One-third constitute the urban poor in crowded metropolitan slums
and informal settlements, and increasingly in the smaller industrialising cities. However,

funding for family agriculture, inadequate support services and backlogs in the
distribution of land. Rural and urban income disparities are reinforced by taxation
schemes skewed to benefit the rich in a system resistant to change.
30. Significant gains have been achieved in the government’s implementation of the
Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Programme (CARP) in terms of a more equitable
distribution of productive resources and building the capability of agrarian reform
beneficiaries in agricultural production. Gender sensitivity is evident in the inclusion of
the woman householder’s name in land transfer titles. However, in order to consolidate
and enhance these gains, government needs to ensure the irreversibility of the programme
through legislation, public advocacy and a post-1998 agrarian scenario that generates
breakthroughs in productivity and income generation among the beneficiaries. The 70 per
cent of women agricultural labourers in rice and corn cultivation need also to be
considered in the process since, with the entry of modern farm technology, their work --
transplanting, weeding, harvesting and threshing -- becomes more susceptible to
displacement. The numbers of female family labourers and female hired labour have been
declining since the 1970s.
31. Despite the decline in unemployment from 9.5 per cent in 1995 to 7.7 in 1997, a growing
pattern of closure, layoffs and job rotation, attributable in large measure to the currency
crisis, has introduced a worrisome note. There now exists what can be termed a job
crisis.15 From January 1 to March 15, 1998, 32,045 workers were affected through 832
company closures. In contrast, for the whole year of 1997, only 59,861 were affected in
1,103 companies. This means that more than half of the total number of workers affected
in 1997 suffered the same consequences in less than three months in 1998. It is feared that
the situation is will worsen in the second and third quarters of 1998. This downtrend in
the labour market is mirrored by the decline in the GNP growth rate which went from
5.68 percent in 1996 to 4.97% in 1997. The outlook for 1998 sees a 3-4 percent GNP
growth rate at best.16 For women, this situation poses serious consequences. Although
earlier declines in unemployment have recently been reversed to a rate of 8.4 percent in
early 1998, women have consistently experienced higher unemployment levels than men
(12.2% vs. 8.3% in 1956 to 10.7% vs. 9.2% by 1994).
32. The segmentation of the labour market and the stagnation of the economy from the 1980s
on to 1992 likely explain this poor performance. Underemployment increased slightly
from 21.1% in 1997 to 21.7% in 1998. One can expect this to increase even further as
many of the newly unemployed flow into the informal sector, the employer of last resort.

33. Also affected by recent economic growth strategies and further aggravated by the
financial crisis has been the environment. Air and water quality has deteriorated rapidly,
especially in urban areas, and water shortages have become acute. The El Niño
phenomenon has spawned widespread drought and near starvation in several regions,
notably Mindanao. Pollution from industrial and human wastes, soil and chemical runoff, overexploitation of coastal resources, illegal and destructive fishing practices,
population pressure and uncontrolled tourism development have seriously degraded
coastal zones and depleted fish and other marine resources.
34. Forests are critically endangered. The Philippine forest cover decreased from
approximately 21 million hectares (70% of total land area) in the 1900’s to 5.2 million
hectares in the mid-1990’s, of which only 800,000 hectares shelter the last remaining old
growth forests and many endangered animal and plant species. Over the past 90 years,
commercial logging decimated 16 million hectares of forest. At the height of
deforestation during the 1970’s, forests disappeared at a rate of 300,000 hectares a year.
With 46 timber licensees in 1994, the projected deforestation rate stood at 100,000
hectares per year. At today’s deforestation levels, the remaining primary forests can easily
be consumed in five years. It is alarming therefore, that there are current timber licenses
that will expire only in 2011, some 14 years from now. Reforestation efforts have found
new support in community based approaches to upland resource management, but they
are still too limited in scale to turn the tide. Of all areas reforested from 1988 to 1991,
only 39,000 hectares of trees have survived. 17 Barely five percent of the country’s coral
reefs remain in excellent condition. About 30-50 per cent of sea grass beds have been lost
in the last 50 years and mangrove areas have receded by about 80 percent in the last 75
years. An estimated 50% of national parks are no longer biologically important.18
35. Poor Filipinos are worst affected by deteriorating environmental quality, because they
depend greatly on natural resources for livelihood, lack adequate health care in the face of
illness caused by chemical pollution, and are often the most affected victims of natural
disasters aggravated by environmental deterioration. Food security is under threat with
the fall in food self-sufficiency and nutritional standards due to rapid population growth,
poverty and constraints in the agriculture sector including poor infrastructure and support

36. One key to the consolidation of socio-economic gains is sound governance. In the wake
of devolved functions under the Local Government Code of 1992, national government
agencies are reconfiguring their roles. At the same time, newly empowered local
government units are trying to respond creatively and effectively to the needs of their
constituents. The vast majority of LGUs, however, still lack the appropriate structures,
management systems, resources, leadership and technical competence to meet the
complex requirements of decentralised governance. NGO efforts have moved strongly
toward organising and educating poorer residents of barangays (villages), towns, cities
and provinces to understand their rights and take advantage of new opportunities for a
transparent and responsive mode of governance.
37. As more women are gradually winning local government elections, there is an
expectation that basic needs and related social issues will feature more significantly in
this last bastion of male domination. While many successful women candidates
apparently derive their power from husbands or fathers no longer eligible to run, their
occupation of key elective positions offers grounds for optimism. Nine, or 12 per cent, of
the 76 provincial governors in 1995 were women, up from 5 in 1992. Vice-Governors
included 12 (16 %), an increase of 6 since 1992. Of 1536 Municipal Mayors in 1995, 125
(or 8.14 %) were women, with a similar percentage shown for Vice-Mayors. The smallest
proportion of female local chief executives is in the cities, which in 1995 elected only 3

elected women mayors and vice-mayors in cities and municipalities. Although Filipino
women are more and more successfully contesting Barangay Council, or village level
seats, they nonetheless remain a small minority among male incumbents at all levels.
38. At the national level in 1995, women held four out of the 24 Senate positions and 21 of
the 203 Representatives posts. The number of women in the national bureaucracy give
cause for optimism in that they occupy 28.8 per cent of the top policy positions, a statistic
which accounts for the relatively high ranking of the Philippines in the Gender
Empowerment Measure.19 The 20,000 development NGOs, whose laudable efforts span
the range from grassroots organising to national level advocacy for policy changes, also
deserve mention here for their large number of women leaders and members.
39. The election of a new administration in 1998 under incoming President Joseph Ejercito
Estrada, who campaigned on a platform prioritising the needs of the poor, offers new
hope for the disadvantaged basic sectors. His early statements predict a focus on food
security, housing the poor and liberalised market, trade and investment policies. The
innovative party list system, while poorly understood by the electorate, has generated new
representation of the basic sectors in Congress. Progressive leaders understand that
government thinking needs to go beyond employment and social safety nets to
substantially increased human resource development through training, retraining, credit,
community organisation, and access to basic services, like health, nutrition, education,
sanitation and shelter. United Nations support can prove instrumental in building up the

 40. In summary, the Philippines has shown an impressive economic turnaround since 1992,
and has moved more strongly in the direction of democratic governance, gender
empowerment and sustainable human development. It also appears to be weathering the
economic shock of the currency crisis in somewhat better form than its neighbours in the
region, owing in part to effective government measures, including the passage of
important legislation, as well as to its late entry into the stage of market liberalisation.
Nonetheless, Philippine society faces serious challenges as it moves into the 21st century,
a realisation that must correspondingly affect the nature and procedures of the UN
Development Assistance Framework.

III. LESSONS LEARNED FROM UN DEVELOPMENT CO-OPERATION
43. The many years of UN development co-operation in the Philippines have generated too
many important lessons for a complete listing here. Those derived from past and current
inter-agency collaborative efforts are thus highlighted as most pertinent to UNDAF
concerns. In order to identify viable areas and procedures for more integrated
collaboration through UNDAF, the Country Team reviewed the actual forms and extent
of collaboration already experienced.
44. The results suggested that successful outcomes were most evident when two or three UN
partners were involved. (See Figure 4). It was also observed, however, that existing
modes of collaboration emphasised information sharing on complementary but essentially
discrete projects, rather than actually planning and implementing together. To achieve
more synergistic action, it appeared that specific programmes and projects needed to be
identified in terms of their collaborative potential, with actual steps toward
implementation carefully defined. Noteworthy programmes that drew in five or more
partners usually carried a sense of urgency, as in disaster management involving ILO,
UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, and WFP; or HIV/AIDS, which brought together all the
agencies through UNAIDS. Another ingredient for successful collaboration among
multi-faceted partners entailed the presence of an enthusiastic full-time co-ordinator and
institutional “champion,” eager to move the process forward and able to create a
nurturing work environment. UNAIDS in the Philippines was a case in point.
45. Utilising the Country Strategy Note facilitated individual agency programming that
combined a healthy diversity with greater convergence. This enabled the groups to favour
a synergistic outcome as they moved from information sharing and ad-hoc
complementation to genuine collaboration. It is important to recognise the constraints that
will make UNDAF implementation problematic unless they are satisfactorily addressed.
These include differences among the agencies, like levels of decentralisation and
decision-making, administrative practices, financial and administrative procedures,
funding mechanisms, overlapping mandates, long-standing inter-agency rivalries and
tensions, time and resource constraints, other work demands, the lack of recognition for
those engaged in collaborative behaviour, and the unclear roles of government, donors,
and civil society in the UNDAF process.
46. Scepticism about the views and commitments of other members of the Country Team can
be significantly reduced through well-planned and -facilitated two- to three-day live-in
workshops, as shown in the January gathering. Intensive consultations in a pleasant and
restful setting enabled the group to address and clarify their differences, and overcome
many of these through working out agreements or acceptable compromises. The January
workshop reduced considerably the group’s earlier scepticism about the feasibility of
heightened collaboration and generated new levels of understanding and enthusiasm
about the UNDAF process.20
47. Major criteria for UNDAF’s success agreed upon by agency heads are the following:
• a sense of priority at country level
• focused, agreed-upon objectives
• a problem-solving orientation
• the availability of additional resources earmarked for testing promising initiatives
• an agency “champion” in each priority area
• top management commitment
• focused tasks and concrete outcomes
• collaborative activities built into the work programmes of agency heads and staff
focal points.
48. Harmonising programme cycles as part of the UNDAF process is an issue that must be
addressed at Headquarters levels. For the JCGP agencies, in particular, despite efforts
toward synchronisation at the country level, differing time frames have been prescribed
by their respective governing boards and Headquarters. Also problematic is the difficulty
of bringing UN agency three- to five-year cycles in line with the government’s six-year
time frame. These cycle inconsistencies undermine the value of UNDAF as a common
response to supporting national priorities and compromise effective co-ordination and
efficient resource allocation.
49. Country level collaboration will be further reinforced if incentives are built into the
system to encourage working together. To this end, it has been agreed that participation in
Inter-agency Working Groups will be built into the annual work plans of agency staff.
50. Since many, if not most, of the areas in which UN programmes are operating deal with
problems where standard blueprint solutions do not exist, there is a need to build
maximum flexibility into programmes to allow for participatory decision making. This
calls for a learning process approach, which can adjust activities in the course of
implementation for greater responsiveness to evolving goals and situational realities. This
approach contrasts with the more traditional blueprint approach that prescribes an overly
rigid framework of pre-determined outputs and work plans.
51. Specialised agencies, like FAO, ILO, UNHCR, UNIDO and WHO have a more generally
defined work programme than their JCGP Country Team members. Hence, they may
have more flexibility in linking up with other UN agencies to design and develop multisectoral, collaborative projects.
52. Agencies not based in the country but supporting programmes in it face special problems
of collaboration. There is a critical need to establish and maintain systematic
communication between the resident Country Team members and the overseas members,
and to organise timely communications regarding meetings, events and matters calling for
the latter’s inputs. The Resident Co-ordinator’s interest and involvement in pursuing this
is particularly important.21
IV. MOVING TOWARD A COMMON UNDAF FRAMEWORK
The United Nations in the Philippines
53. The UN system enjoys a unique and distinctive character in the overall development
context of the country because of the strong support extended by the Philippines for its
programmes and activities. The Philippines is one of the founding members of the United
Nations. Building on the legacy of pro-active advocacy begun by Filipino diplomats to the
United Nations, such as Carlos P. Romulo, Rafael Salas and Domingo Siazon, Philippine
governmental and non-governmental delegations have been active in preparing for the
global conferences. The Philippines has taken its commitments at these conferences
seriously, as indicated by the follow-up actions and mechanisms pursued by government
and civil society. It was one of the first countries after the Rio Summit to develop its own
localised Agenda 21. The Philippine Plan for Gender Responsive Development: 1995-
2025 represents one of the most extensive plans in Southeast Asia for the follow-up of the
Beijing Conference. And as a framework for integrating various human development
commitments in these global conferences, the Philippines Social Reform Agenda is a
trend-setter within the region.
54. The presence of UN Country Team agencies in the Philippines derives from their
representing the United Nations and promoting its mandates for peace, justice and
development. Government and non-government organisations see the UN System as a
source of international perspectives and experience on these issues; a purveyor of global
concerns, such as women’s participation and sustainable human development; and an
effective catalyst in mobilising resources from other multilateral and bilateral agencies for
key government and civil society programmes. Its multilateral status means that its
international civil servants maintain their loyalty to international ideals rather than to
promoting specific country interests.
55. Given competing needs in the face of limited resources, the UN system helps the
government make more effective and efficient use of these resources. Its members are
keenly interested in heightening the relevance of UN support to the country’s
development priorities, and in improving co-ordination among UN agencies through
agreed-upon strategies. Keenly aware of the small financial contributions of UN agencies
relative to overall development assistance to the Philippines (0.8 % for JCGP agencies),
the UN System focuses on the human development, social justice and peace concerns
distinctive of its global mandate. The commitment of the new Ejercito Estrada
Administration to focus on the needs of the poor while maintaining overall economic and
environmental progress, opens up promising avenues for UNCT action.22
Building on Existing UN Collaboration
56. While each UN agency has its distinct mandate, some elements complement one another
so effectively that the principals make natural partners in the UNDAF process. Some
examples are in order. UNFPA’s reproductive health focus, which includes family
planning, human sexuality, violence against women, adolescent health and youth
development and gender issues, links closely with UNICEF’s concerns around safe
motherhood, maternal and child health, the education and nutritional needs of women, the
girl child, and healthy lifestyles for adolescents. WHO likewise shares many of
UNFPA’s and UNICEF’s concerns. ILO’s attention to indigenous communities is echoed
in virtually all other agency programmes, while collaboration with WHO focuses on
occupational health. ILO’s role in helping Filipino migrant workers reintegrate into
Philippine life, improve enterprise development and worker protection, links with
UNIDO’s technical assistance in small and medium sized enterprises. UNIDO in turn has
a natural ally in UNDP through programmes aimed at developing strategies, policies and
institutions for global economic integration, international competitiveness, technology
transfer and environmental protection.
57. FAO finds correspondence in UNIDO’s linking agro-industry with farmers for rural
industrial development, UNDP support to agrarian reform, and UNICEF’s and WHO’s
involvement in the nutrition of children and women. UNDP’s thrusts in poverty
alleviation, assistance to local governance, environmental regeneration, disaster planning,
disseminating the Human Development Index and Minimum Basic Needs indicators,
represent areas that complement other agency programmes. Its move in the direction of
urban informal and micro-enterprises calls for contact with ILO. Educating the nation on
sustainable development through the school system and out-of-school training
programmes makes UNDP a natural partner of UNESCO and UNICEF. Convergence is
evident between UNFPA, UNHCR, UNICEF and WHO for the well-being of refugee
populations. Virtually the entire team is involved in the UN system’s collaboration for
post-conflict peace and development in Mindanao. UNAIDS represents the most
integrated programme of activities to date, with UN agency involvement in HIV/AIDS
dating back to the 1980s. After WHO and the Government worked out the First Medium
Term plan on HIV/AIDS, other agencies added the technical and financial resource,
training and capacity development needed by several new Philippine partners. (For a
more complete but still indicative listing, see Figure 5.)
58. The mandates and approaches taken by the various agencies thus incorporate the roots of
collaboration. All believe capacity building and technical assistance to be essential. All
express an interest in helping local governments and NGO partners achieve improved
implementation capacities, especially in expanding access of the poor to basic services.
Policy analysis, monitoring and evaluation and regular utilisation of common indicators
and baseline data are also skills that would benefit from GO-NGO-PO partnerships. In
addition to ongoing programme collaboration, UN agencies have had the advantage of
extensive interaction in the follow-up to over ten global conferences from 1990 to 1997.
Undertaking the UNDAF process will enable each agency to bring to the table its23
expertise in advocacy skills, service delivery, capacity building and technical assistance.
The UNDAF process is underway when cohesive UN family members act in concert to
conceptualise problems, plan, implement and monitor projects and programmes together.
Strategic and Priority Areas for Co-operation and Cross-Cutting Themes for UN
Collaboration (See also Figure 5.)
59. UNCT choices of strategic and priority areas for UNDAF collaboration dovetail with
Government-UN System agreements on development co-operation. Each strategic area
includes one or more priority action sets, yielding a total of 12. Each has an agency head
as its convenor. Twelve Inter-Agency Working Groups (IAWG) have been organised to
work out the terms of reference, tasks and activities pertinent to each priority set. The first
strategic area covers four priority groups pursuing social equity in the growth process.
The second also entails four priority groups focusing on capacity building, justice and
human development as building blocks for people’s well being. The third seeks a balance
between population, resources and environment as they relate to two priority groups, with
a view toward sustainable human development. Effective people’s participation and
responsive local government as essential components of national development are
emphasised in the fourth priority set, while the fifth concentrates inter-agency efforts in
Mindanao. These are in turn affected by five cross-cutting themes that all 12 Working
Groups will build into their discussions and work plans.

60. The convenor of each IAWG is responsible for guiding his or her IAWG toward
convergent activities, monitoring progress and communicating the results to the Country
Team at the regular monthly UN meetings or other appropriate gatherings. Together with
the agency focal points in the IAWG, the convenor will establish the terms of reference
and annual work plans. IAWGs are expected to become operational no later than the
second quarter of 1998. Convenors will facilitate collaboration between agencies with
convergent programmes. They are committed to chairing the meetings themselves
throughout the life of the IAWG, and not delegate that task to a staff member.
61. The implementation process is an iterative one that will guide the UNCT as it undertakes
future programmes and projects. For example, a world-wide interest in good governance,
which also emerges in the Philippines, has led to an emphasis on capacity building for
local government units. This will be enriched and strengthened by activities associated
with a projected World Conference on Governance. On the child labour front, joint
monitoring is getting underway through ILO and UNICEF. Periodic reviews will be held
by the UNCT to assess how agency programmes are complementing one another with
synergistic outcomes, or how they are changing in the new working environment.
Integration of the cross-cutting issues, especially the gender-related ones, into all
programmes will also be carefully monitored. Should it become evident as the process
evolves that twelve working groups are simply too numerous to manage, some of them
might be merged, for example, Smeall and Medium Enterprises with Industry and
Environment. This would illustrate the principle behind the IAWGs, namely, that they
serve as flexible mechanisms for evolving a convergent learning approach aimed at
heightening the impact of UN development assistance in the Philippines.
Monitoring and Evaluation
62. The results of the IAWGs will be closely monitored by the agency-head convenor, who
will also make periodic progress reports at selected Country Team monthly meetings.25
There he or she can raise special points of interest and problems relevant to collaboration,
as identified in the IAWG experience. During these discussions, points related to the
broader strategic areas of co-operation will also be reviewed. Each monthly meeting will
feature one of the 12 groups, ensuring that all of them have the opportunity within the
year to review lessons learned with the entire Team, and to propose needed programme,
policy, administrative or financial changes. The review will also cover the cross-cutting
themes. These decisions emphasise the importance the Country Team attaches to the
IAWGs as strategic mechanisms for institutionalising UNDAF collaboration in practical
ways, drawing on actual programmatic and administrative experience.
63. The outcome of this central and pivotal exercise should yield programmes and projects
that bring several UN agencies together simultaneously, along with their national partners
and donors, in needs identification, programme development and design, implementation,
and monitoring and evaluation. The process of collaboration itself will be carefully
monitored for lessons learned and any mid-course corrections needed. Among the results
will be a series of reports on what works in inter-agency collaboration to produce a
synergistic impact, and what measures are needed to overcome constraints. At the same
time, on-going assessments will clarify the extent to which UN assistance may also be
undermined by certain forms of collaboration, and what decisions at field and
headquarters levels need to be taken regarding this reality.
64. Country programme reviews will be conducted at mid-term and end-of-cycle points, with
government, civil society partners, private sector participants, donors and invited
external resource persons. Results will be assessed in terms of outcomes and impact
within the priority areas for collaboration, taking into consideration also single- and
multi-agency projects. They will examine contributions to national priorities as well as to
the overall co-ordination of the UN system. Criteria for monitoring and evaluation will be
sharpened through this experience. The overall results will become the basis for further
discussions by the Country Team toward setting new directions or refining existing
strategies in the next programme cycle.
65. Annual work plans of the Resident Co-ordinator and the Country Management Team will
build on a systematic yearly assessment of the previous year’s activities and
achievements, a review of the country situation and progress in the development of
country programmes and projects, together with a critical examination of Inter Agency
Working Group results and follow-up measures.
66. The key implementors of the UNDAF process are the Resident Co-ordinator and the UN
Country Team, composed of agency and programme heads: the JCGP agencies -- UNDP,
UNFPA, and UNICEF, the specialised agencies -- FAO, ILO, UNESCO, UNIDO, WHO
and UNHCR and UNAIDS. The Resident Co-ordinator, who convenes and leads the UN
system, will be expected to play a key role in facilitating the UNDAF collaboration in the
interests of Philippine development and more effective UN delivery of services,
intellectual and technical expertise, and funds.
67. The benefits of collaboration, evidenced also in improved individual agency outputs, have
been articulated by the Country Team:26
• harmony through teamwork that establishes common priorities in a balanced and
cohesive manner for easier incorporation into new country programme planning
and implementation
• effectiveness and efficiency that add value to UN system efforts, consistency in
technical and policy advice, expanded programme coverage and more effective
use of resources.
68. This anticipated synergy will foster an enhanced image of the UN among partners and
donors, bring about a more holistic programme outcome, improve advocacy efforts and
strengthen resource mobilisation. At the same time, costs have to be considered, among
them, management and staff time, diminished identity and autonomy of agencies leading
to a weakening of traditional constituencies, diluted accountability, complicated financial
management, less flexibility to carry out agency mandates, and a possible drop in
programme quality to the lowest common denominator. Possible ways of addressing these
will have to be considered as the UN Country Team gains experience in collaboration.
69. This instructive cost-benefit assessment argues in favour of a modest start for UNDAF,
featuring learning by doing. Such a strategy would heighten success and avoid
undermining agency strengths. As it was felt important to preserve each agency’s identity
and autonomy while interacting through UNDAF, the Country Team seeks to:
• identify clearly the activities implemented by each agency engaged in a
collaborative programme or project
• highlight those areas of a programme or project in which each agency has a
comparative advantage, and
• write UNDAF documents in an enabling manner, incorporating a careful review
of UN-assisted country programmes and projects.
